subject: pharmacology
title: Antihypertensive drugs

steps.tx: Antihypertensive drugs lower pressure by reducing volume, vascular resistance, cardiac output, or renin signalling. First line treatment uses **thiazide like diuretics**, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and **calcium channel blockers**, while beta blockers suit compelling cardiac indications. All effective classes prevent stroke and heart failure when pressure falls, and the achieved pressure matters more than the brand name. Single pill combinations improve control and adherence far better than pushing one drug to its maximum dose alone.
steps.say: First line treatment can lower pressure through complementary mechanisms in most patients. Diuretics reduce volume while calcium blockers dilate arteries. Drugs blocking the renin system protect kidneys and hearts. Combination pills control pressure in most patients effectively. The achieved pressure matters more than the brand chosen.

vis.alt: Blood pressure equals cardiac output times resistance, controlled at five sites: volume with thiazide-like diuretics, renin with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone as fourth agent, arteries with dihydropyridine calcium blockers, heart with rate-limiting blockers. Organ damage needs controlled IV reduction.
vis.caption: Five sites, three first-line classes; spironolactone is the proven fourth.

steps.tx: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown, which protects diabetic kidneys and failing hearts. Their costs include **dry cough** from bradykinin, rare **angioedema**, fetal harm that forbids pregnancy use, and rises in potassium and creatinine that need blood checks after starting. ARBs block the receptor instead, spare the cough, but share fetal and potassium cautions. Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB routinely harms more than it helps and should be avoided.
steps.say: ACE inhibitors can protect kidneys and hearts in many patients treated. Bradykinin accumulation causes the characteristic dry cough. Angioedema is rare but threatens the airway dangerously. Potassium and creatinine must be checked after starting treatment. Combining both renin blockers routinely causes more harm than benefit.

steps.tx: Calcium channel blockers divide by their main site of action. **Dihydropyridines** such as amlodipine dilate arteries and cause ankle oedema, flushing, and gum hypertrophy, while **verapamil** and diltiazem slow conduction and contractility for rate control and must be combined cautiously with beta blockers. Beta blockers now serve hypertension mainly when coronary disease, heart failure, or rate control also needs treatment, because uncomplicated elderly stroke prevention trailed rivals while bronchospasm, fatigue, and masking of hypoglycaemia remain real costs.
steps.say: Amlodipine dilates arteries and commonly swells the ankles. Verapamil slows conduction and reduces cardiac contractility. Combining rate limiting drugs carelessly can block conduction dangerously. Beta blockers help most when the heart also needs treatment. Their metabolic and bronchospasm costs are limits on routine use in practice.

steps.tx: This photograph shows bilateral pitting **ankle oedema** with an inset of enlarged gums during amlodipine treatment. Both findings are signature adverse effects of **dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers**, caused by preferential arteriolar dilatation rather than fluid retention or heart failure. In exams, painless ankle swelling after starting amlodipine should not automatically trigger diuretics or heart failure treatment, and gum hypertrophy is a classic pairing that identifies the drug class immediately.
steps.say: This photograph shows pitting swelling around both ankles clearly. The inset is a view of overgrown gums in the same drug context. Amlodipine causes both effects through arterial dilatation and tissue changes. The swelling does not automatically mean heart failure has developed. Recognising the pairing helps students identify the drug class quickly.

vis.caption: Amlodipine adverse effects with ankle oedema. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Resistant hypertension means pressure remains uncontrolled on three drugs including a diuretic. **Spironolactone** is the proven fourth agent before secondary causes are hunted, including primary aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, sleep apnoea, thyroid disease, and drug culprits such as NSAIDs, steroids, contraceptives, and liquorice. Pregnancy hypertension uses **methyldopa**, labetalol, and nifedipine, while ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin blockers are fetotoxic and should stop before conception wherever possible in planned pregnancy.
steps.say: Resistant hypertension remains uncontrolled despite three appropriate drugs. Spironolactone is the proven fourth drug for most patients. Secondary causes should be hunted when clues appear. Pregnancy needs drugs with established fetal safety. Fetotoxic renin blockers must stop before conception whenever possible.

right.title: Secondary clues
points: Young, resistant, bruits, low potassium, snoring

steps.tx: **Hypertensive emergencies** with organ damage need controlled intravenous reduction in a monitored setting. Encephalopathy, aortic dissection, and pulmonary oedema define true emergencies, while severe asymptomatic hypertension needs oral titration and follow up rather than a precipitous drop that injures adapted organs. Older pearls include methyldopa causing positive Coombs tests, **clonidine rebound** after sudden withdrawal, hydralazine causing a lupus like syndrome, and minoxidil causing fluid retention with hirsutism. Every regimen ends with home readings, adherence review, and electrolyte and kidney surveillance regularly.
steps.say: Organ damage is the defining feature of a true hypertensive emergency. Controlled intravenous treatment protects organs without causing ischaemia. Severe pressure without damage needs steady oral treatment instead. Dropping pressure too fast starves chronically adapted organs. Home readings and blood tests confirm safe long term control.
